ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9 (Alberta), ss 21.1-21.5 and s 114 (Significant Individual / director registers), as amended by the Business Corporations Amendment Act, 2018, SA 2018, c 19; Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, SC 2000, c 17 (PCMLTFA) and associated PCMLTFR; Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46, Part II.1 (terrorist financing); Special Economic Measures Act, SC 1992, c 17; United Nations Act, RSC 1985, c U-2; federal CBCA, RSC 1985, c C-44, s 21.1 if federal incorporation is elected. The Alberta ISC register is kept at the corporation's records office, is not filed for public inspection, and must be produced to police, CRA, FINTRAC, and other authorized authorities upon lawful demand. Shareholders and creditors have qualified inspection rights under ABCA s 21.4.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, officers, UBOs, and settlement account signatories against the consolidated UN Security Council sanctions list, Canadian SEMA and United Nations Act regulations administered by Global Affairs Canada, OFAC SDN and CAPTA lists (required for USD ACH and wire rails through Mercury), and FINTRAC advisories. PEP determination and enhanced review must follow PCMLTFR s 11.12, covering foreign PEPs, domestic PEPs, heads of international organizations, family members, and close associates. Beneficial ownership must be verified to the 25% threshold per ABCA ss 21.1-21.5 with documented source of funds and risk rating; any high-risk jurisdiction nexus or PEP match requires enhanced due diligence and senior management approval. All records retained for a minimum of five years under PCMLTFA.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry via the Alberta Business Registry portal (albertaca.ca); legacy CORES portal discontinued
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names must use letters of the English or French alphabet, Arabic numerals, or a permissible combination; foreign-script trade names must be submitted in a romanized transliteration and may be reflected as an extra-provincial trade name where applicable under ABCA Name Regulations
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Bank; Trust; Trustco; Insurance; Assurance; Loan; Credit Union; University; College; Institute; Lawyer; Barrister; Solicitor; Accountant; Engineer; Architect; Royal; Crown; Alberta (government affiliation implication); Canada or Canadian (federal approval required)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: No extension is available for an expired NUANS report; the applicant must obtain a fresh NUANS search report (statutory fee CA$10) and refile. Upon rejection, the applicant may request written reasons from the Registrar of Corporations, submit a revised distinctive name, or seek ministerial consent for a sensitive token under the ABCA Name Regulations. If the registrar maintains the refusal, the applicant may apply for judicial review to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta after exhausting registrar reconsideration; name-conflict precedence disputes are adjudicated under ABCA Name Regulations ss 14-19.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Acceptable only where the provider supplies a physical street address in Alberta, consents to service of process, and accepts legal documents; post office boxes are prohibited. For a pure digital media buying and affiliate lead generation operation with no physical inventory or premises, a virtual registered office is commercially adequate, provided that CRA GST place-of-supply rules and corporate residence substance are separately managed.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low to moderate: approximately 10-15% probability within the first 24 months of unannounced substance verification by CRA (GST/QST audits) or by the onboarding financial institution under enhanced due diligence; the Alberta Corporate Registry does not conduct routine physical inspections.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9 (ABCA), ss. 4-5 (incorporation), 8 (certificate of incorporation), 45 (articles), 102 (registered office), 104-105 (share records), 125 (board of directors)
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta (Corporate Registry Operations)
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation, together with Notice of Registered Office and Notice of Directors (Alberta corporate formation filing package)
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital is prescribed under the ABCA. Authorized share capital is set in the articles; shares may be issued for such consideration as the directors determine. No escrow account or capital deposit is required. A physical registered office address in Alberta must be maintained and service of process may be accepted there.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, by the board of directors effective as of [date], that: 1. The incorporator's subscription contract for 100 common shares without par value, at CAD 0.01 per share, is hereby ratified, accepted, and issued as fully paid to the sole incorporator, to be recorded in the share register. 2. The registered office of the corporation shall be lawfully maintained at [registered office address] in the Province of Alberta, and [law firm/corporate service provider] is authorized to accept service of process. 3. The following person is appointed as the sole director until the next annual general meeting: [director]. The following officers are appointed: [president], [secretary], [treasurer]. 4. The corporation may engage in ISIC 7310 digital advertising and all related lawful activities. Certified by the corporate secretary.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry NUANS system (via Service Alberta or an authorized registry agent)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS preliminary name search to verify availability, select a corporate designation (Inc., Corp., or Ltd.), and reserve the proposed name for up to 90 days. Submit the reservation before preparing articles of incorporation.
required_dossiers: Directors' consent to act, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the proposed name is rejected or is confusingly similar to an existing name, file an alternate name reservation or request a name amendment before submitting the articles of incorporation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation and Submission of Articles of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry online portal or authorized Alberta registry agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete and file the Articles of Incorporation, Notice of Registered Office, and Notice of Directors. Ensure all signatures are present; if submitting paper form, have signatures notarized. Pay the applicable filing fee at submission.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registry issues a deficiency notice or query, cure the stated errors and resubmit the corrected filing within the prescribed registry time limit; any outstanding fee must be paid before re-processing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After the registry approves the filing package, the Certificate of Incorporation is issued and the corporation comes into legal existence. Verify the certificate details and retrieve the corporate registry record from the Alberta Corporate Registration System.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation issued by the registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If issuance is delayed, submit a service request to the registry for expedited processing; if the certificate contains an error, file a Statement of Correction to amend the corporate record.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Organizational Meeting and First Board Resolution
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the newly formed corporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Hold the statutory first board meeting after incorporation. Adopt by-laws, ratify pre-incorporation contracts, approve the issuance of shares to the incorporator, appoint officers, adopt the registered office, and pass the pro-forma first board resolution contained in this dossier.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a procedural defect is identified, cure it by unanimous board consent or by a subsequent remedial board resolution, and amend the corporate minute book accordingly.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: CRA Business Number Registration and Alberta Corporate Tax Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration, as applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register for the CRA Business Number (RT0001) and any required corporate tax accounts using the Business Registration Online service. Update the Alberta corporate registry annual return profile and confirm the registered office information.
required_dossiers: Identity documents of directors and officers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the tax registration is delayed or queried, contact the CRA business window to correct information, resubmit through Business Registration Online, or file directly with the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Municipal business licensing department in the city of the registered office (e.g., City of Calgary Licensing Services or City of Edmonton Business Licensing); no provincial or federal industrial licensing board applies to ISIC 7310 digital advertising media arbitrage.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Municipal General Business Licence, or Home Occupation Business Licence if operating from a residential premises; a separate advertising industry permit is not required.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Alberta Environment and Protected Areas (AEPA) and Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC), as applicable
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — the registered activity is an administrative and digital media-buying operation with no physical industrial facility; no EIA is triggered.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable for industrial wastewater, VOCs, or process emissions. If leased office space is used, comply with municipal waste disposal, indoor air quality, electrical safety, and landlord environmental covenants; no regulated discharge points exist.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety certification under the Alberta Fire Code, a building occupancy permit for the registered office, and occupational health and safety clearance under Alberta's Occupational Health and Safety Act, RSA 2017, c O-2.1. Maintain workers' compensation coverage with the Workers' Compensation Board of Alberta (WCB-Alberta) if employees are engaged.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) – National portal: CRA My Business Account (MyBA) at canada.ca/en/revenue-agency.html
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Foreign entities not otherwise required to obtain a Canadian TIN must apply for a CRA Business Number (BN/RT) via the CRA Business Registration Online service or by paper form RC1. For GST/HST purposes, the BN is appended with the 'RT' program account. Non-resident corporations carrying on business in Canada through a permanent establishment or deriving Canadian-source income must register for income tax under the BN and file T2 returns. The procedure requires proof of incorporation, Canadian address for service (if applicable), and identification of the Canadian agent or permanent establishment contact. Online registration is immediate for most non-resident corporate applicants without a compliance hold; otherwise, mailing to the applicable CRA tax centre with supporting documents is accepted. A separate provincial registration for Alberta Corporate Tax is not generally required when the federal BN is used for Alberta corporate income tax purposes, but a provincial corporate tax account (CRA administered for Alberta) is established automatically via the T2 corporate income tax registration process.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation. A Canadian Business Corporation (federal or Alberta provincial) is a separate legal person and is a resident corporation if incorporated in Canada under the Income Tax Act (ITA). It is subject to Part I tax on worldwide income, unless an exception for non-resident corporations applies. The default classification under the ITA is a taxable corporation, not a pass-through entity, and there is no general check-the-box regime analogous to the US. Alberta does not levy a separate provincial corporate income tax beyond the federal-provincial integrated tax collection: under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, Alberta uses a single flat rate (currently 8%) applied to taxable income allocated to Alberta, collected by the CRA under the Tax Collection Agreements. Territorial scope for a Canadian-incorporated company is full residence-based taxation; Alberta allocation rules apply for corporate income where a permanent establishment exists in Alberta.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No check-the-box classification election is available for federal or Alberta corporate tax purposes. The only entity classification election applicable to corporations is under the 'Canadian-controlled private corporation' (CCPC) status, which arises statutorily if conditions are met (all shares owned by Canadian residents and no public corporation status). There is no hybrid mismatch election for ordinary corporations; however, for cross-border tax planning, an election may be made under subsection 216(1) ITA for a non-resident corporation’s rental income, or under section 216.1 for property gains, and certain treaty-based returns (section 115, 116 and 128.1) require specific filings. In the context of business corporations, an election under section 89 ITA or the capital dividend account may be utilized, but this does not alter entity classification for income tax. For GST/HST purposes, a non-resident corporation may elect to use a branch office registration instead of establishing a Canadian permanent establishment under the Simplified GST/HST Registration regime for non-residents (option to rebate GST/HST on certain inputs), but this does not change the default corporate income tax classification.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) / Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) - Canada; Alberta imposes no provincial sales tax; federal GST at 5% applies. For Alberta, only the federal GST is applicable; no Alberta provincial sales tax or provincial HST component. For supplies of digital advertising and media-buying services involving Canadian recipients, the place-of-supply rules in the Excise Tax Act (ETA) deem the supply to be made in Canada if the recipient is a Canadian resident, and the supplier must register for GST/HST if it is a non-resident entity carrying on business in Canada or engaged in commercial activity in Canada. However, an exemption applies to non-resident persons that are not registered and do not carry on business in Canada for supplies of certain 'intangible personal property' and services made to Canadian recipients only if the supply is not made by a person that is required to register. The 'non-resident simplified GST/HST registration' is available for non-resident suppliers making taxable supplies in Canada, allowing recovery of input tax credits.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: General GST/HST registration threshold is CAD 30,000 in taxable supplies per calendar quarter (i.e., over 4 consecutive calendar quarters exceeding CAD 30,000). For non-resident persons with no permanent establishment in Canada, the threshold is CAD 30,000 unless the person is a 'registrant' by election or supplies 'advertising services' or 'digital goods/services' to Canadian recipients. Special mandatory registration rules apply to non-resident suppliers of 'digital services' (GST/HST on e-commerce, effective July 1, 2021) and to suppliers operating a digital platform, where the threshold is CAD 30,000 of gross revenue from Canadian-sourced digital supplies. For the affiliate media-buying sector, if the Canadian counterparty is a registered business, the supplier may be zero-rated under the 'non-resident supplier providing services to a Canadian recipient who is a GST/HST registrant' rule (section 179 of ETA), provided the service is exclusively for supply to a registered recipient. Otherwise, the 5% GST must be charged.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not currently operate a mandatory nationwide electronic invoicing clearance system or real-time fiscal stamping for GST/HST. The CRA accepts electronic invoices and records if they meet the ETA’s prescribed information requirements (set out in the GST/HST Memorandum 8-7 and ETA Regulations). There is no requirement for pre-clearance of invoices by the CRA. However, since 2020, for GST/HST e-commerce rules, platform operators must maintain detailed records of Canadian suppliers’ transactions and may be required to report information to the CRA through the GST/HST E-Commerce Forms (RC5213, RC5214). For large businesses, mandatory electronic filing of GST/HST returns and T2 corporate income tax returns is required if the corporation has gross revenue exceeding CAD 1,000,000 or is a corporate entity required to file electronically. All GST/HST returns generally must be filed and paid electronically using CRA’s GST/HST NETFILE or a registered E-file transmitter; payment may be made by wire transfer or online. The CRA has announced a gradual adoption of Peppol-based e-invoicing standards starting with public sector procurement, but no statutory mandate exists for private B2B transactions in Alberta as of the knowledge cutoff. Digital stamping or real-time clearance is not applicable; instead, the CRA relies on audit-based disclosure of business documents.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: For the affiliate media-buying (ISIC 7310, NAICS 541810) model, zero-rating applies to supplies of services or intangible personal property (including advertising services) exported to non-resident persons if the supply is for use or consumption exclusively outside Canada. Under section 7 of Part V of Schedule VI to the ETA, a supply of a service made by a Canadian entity to a non-resident individual or to a non-resident corporation (that is not a Canadian resident) is zero-rated, provided that the service is not a supply of an exemption listed (e.g., advice, consultation, or some services relating to land in Canada). Advertising services, including digital media buying, affiliate lead generation, and programmatic advertising, are zero-rated under item 7 of Part V if the recipient is a non-resident and the service is not supplied to a Canadian resident or a Canadian branch. Additionally, if the Canadian corporation provides services to a foreign affiliate or non-resident counterpart, the supplier must maintain evidence that the recipient is non-resident and that the service is not 'in connection with real estate situated in Canada' nor 'performed in Canada' under certain deemed supply rules. Where an intermediary Canadian corporation purchases media inventory on behalf of foreign clients, careful documentation is required to demonstrate the supply is made in Canada for zero-rating, as the CRA may treat the service as being a supply to a Canadian-resident advertiser if the Canadian intermediary agrees to indemnify or assume liability. Zero-rating does not require a refund; it allows the supplier to claim input tax credits on inputs without charging output tax. Exporters may claim GST/HST refunds for input tax credits in excess of output tax via the regular ITC refund claim in the GST/HST return or through the Non-Resident Rebate program if applicable. The CRA Form GST189 (General Application for GST/HST Rebate) or standard return must be filed.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (via Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) G13 / CAED - Canadian export declaration; required for goods, but services are evidenced by commercial contracts and invoices)
Export Invoice / Commercial Invoice (in the name of the Canadian exporting entity)
Service Agreement or Master Services Agreement (clearly identifying the non-resident recipient, scope of services, and payment terms)
Bill of Lading or Airway Bill (for goods; not applicable for pure digital services, but for any incidental physical media materials, required)
Inward Remittance Certificate (bank statement showing receipt of foreign currency from the non-resident client; or a wire transfer confirmation)

Non-Resident Confirmation (e.g., foreign business registration, or sworn declaration of non-residency) and, if applicable, a Canadian GST/HST registration number of the recipient when zero-rating is claimed under the registered-recipient rule
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA may audit export zero-rating claims for a period of up to four years (and in cases of neglect, misrepresentation, or fraud, an unlimited period). If the CRA determines that the export zero-rating was claimed in error (e.g., the service was actually consumed in Canada, the recipient was a Canadian resident, the documentation is insufficient, or the supply was not zero-rated due to a subsection 2.1 deemed supply), the CRA will retroactively assess the supplier for uncollected GST/HST, interest, and penalties. Penalties under the ETA include: (i) any person who fails to charge GST/HST when required is liable to pay the uncollected tax; (ii) failure to register may result in a penalty of up to CAD 10,000 (non-resident) or a general penalty of CAD 500 plus late-filing penalties; (iii) knowingly making a false or misleading statement in a return (including a zero-rating claim) is subject to a penalty of 50% of the amount of tax sought to be evaded, plus interest under sections 280 and 285 ETA; (iv) late or deficient remittances accrue daily interest at the prescribed rate plus a late-filing penalty of 1% per month up to 12 months on the unpaid tax. In addition, the Income Tax Act may impose penalties for false statements in corporate returns leading to additional assessments and, in egregious cases, criminal liability for tax evasion. For an affiliate media buying entity, clawback risk is heightened if the CRA determines the business is acting as a principal reselling advertising inventory to a Canadian advertiser through a non-resident affiliate, thereby failing the 'direct' zero-rating test; in such cases, the entire historical GST output tax may be assessed plus interest and penalties. The CRA’s GST/HST Audit Manual directs for export substantiation: copies of contracts, invoices, proof of payment, and proof of the non-resident status of the recipient, and a failure to maintain such books is itself an offense with a penalty of CAD 10,000 under subsection 283.1.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) in coordination with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for currency-related transactional oversight; Canada imposes no central-bank exchange control approval regime.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains a fully convertible currency for both current and capital account transactions, with the Canadian dollar floating freely. No exchange control permit or central bank authorization is required for current account payments, cross-border dividends, management fees, or capital repatriation. However, payments must be supported by contemporaneous commercial documentation, comply with AML/KYC expectations of the receiving and intermediary banks, and satisfy applicable tax withholdings (e.g., Part XIII non-resident withholding tax on dividends, interest, and certain payments). Profit remittance is unrestricted but bank compliance may request documentary evidence of underlying transaction legitimacy, invoicing, and transfer pricing consistency for intra-group payments.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There are no statutory surrender requirements, mandatory conversion ratios, or repatriation timelines for export receipts in Canada. Foreign currency may be retained in domestic or offshore accounts, but where export proceeds are received into a Canadian corporate bank account, the corporate must ensure accurate bookkeeping, FX valuation for tax reporting, and FINTRAC large-dollar reporting thresholds (e.g., $10,000 or equivalent in certain transaction contexts). Non-resident-owned corporations and Canadian corporations with foreign accounts must consider T1135 reporting obligations for specified foreign property if applicable.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Moderate-to-High feasibility for licensed and regulated cross-border payment fintechs such as Wise Platform, Airwallex, and Payoneer, provided they hold applicable money service business (MSB) licenses under Canadian provincial regimes or are operating with a registered foreign MSB in Canada. Canadian fintechs may be used as non-bank settlement vehicles, but cannot substitute for a domestic Schedule I bank account where the corporation requires an escrow-capable custody layer, direct access to Canadian clearing infrastructure, or CAD settlement credibility with counterparties. Offshore EMIs (e.g., U.K. EMIs, EU payment institutions) are viable only as supplemental treasury tools for sub-account management and FX conversion; they should not hold operating capital for media buy settlements due to FINTRAC registration concerns, weaker lender-of-last-resort protection, and lack of CDIC deposit insurance. The entity must maintain a primary corporate operating account at a Canadian Schedule I bank.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote corporate onboarding is generally permitted by Canadian banks under FINTRAC-regulated KYC procedures, but final approval is heavily risk-calibrated. For an Alberta corporation engaged in affiliate media buying (rated Medium-Risk Enhanced), banks may impose: (i) a video conference with at least one authorized signatory and the ultimate beneficial owner to confirm operational substance; (ii) notarized certified copies of corporate documents; (iii) proof of Alberta registered office and business address; and (iv) where the director is non-resident, a physical in-branch interview at a Canadian branch may be required unless a banking relationship with a reputable correspondent is established. A physical presence mandate is most likely where the company is newly incorporated, has no Canadian credit history, and shows high expected transaction velocity through multiple foreign jurisdictions. To avoid delay, the onboarding plan should designate a Canadian-resident director or an experienced corporate services partner with an existing bank relationship.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Newly formed corporation with minimal financial statements seeking to open a bank account for immediate high-volume cross-border media spend
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Alberta Certificate of Incorporation; Articles of Incorporation and bylaws; Certificate of Good Standing; complete register of directors and officers; ultimate beneficial ownership (UBO) declaration identifying all natural persons with 25%+ ownership; projected cash-flow model showing expected monthly media buys and settlement volumes; copies of advertising network master agreements and publisher affiliate agreements; detailed narrative of the affiliate media buying model, including performance attribution methodology; reference letters from existing banking relationships or legal counsel.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident directors or shareholders controlling a Canadian corporation and wiring funds from foreign exchange platforms
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Passport copies and notarized proof of residential address for each director/UBO; source-of-wealth documentation for the funds to be injected (e.g., audited financials, tax records, or executed sale/loan agreements); evidence of legitimate business purpose for the Canadian entity; tax residency certificates and confirmation that no politically exposed person (PEP) risk exists; legal opinion letter from Canadian counsel confirming the corporate governance structure; description of the economic substance and operational presence in Alberta.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-velocity payments to many counterparties in jurisdictions considered higher-risk for fraud or sanctions, common in digital media arbitrage
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Sanctions screening policy and technology controls; approved vendor onboarding checklist for each counterparty; active IP/URL verification for inventory sources; contractual documentation proving each payment is for settled media traffic rather than fund pass-through; detailed ledger of affiliate sub-publisher identity; source-of-funds reconciliation reports; FINTRAC compliance program documentation including employee training records, transaction monitoring protocols, and suspicious transaction reporting (STR) escalation procedure.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Ambiguity in the business description where 'arbitrage' may imply prohibited cross-border structuring or trading of financial instruments
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Business plan prepared in plain language emphasizing performance-based digital advertising, affiliate lead generation, and media buying, not securities arbitrage or cryptocurrency trading; ISIC/NAICS classification confirmation letters from a certified accountant; contracts with ad networks and demand-side platforms; accounting policy note explaining revenue recognition for media arbitrage margin; surrender of the requirement for securities licensing by confirming no trading of financial products and no custody of third-party client funds.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant injection of capital into the Alberta corporation should be executed via SWIFT international wire transfers (MT103) or SWIFT GPI instructions from the shareholder's bank to the Canadian operational or capital escrow account. Remittance instructions must include the corporate legal name, account number, reference to shareholder's name, and a purpose description such as 'Contribution to capital under Canada Business Corporations Act' or 'Subordinated shareholder loan for working capital'. Canadian banks do not require standardized purpose codes, but the outward remitting bank will apply an ISO 20022 purpose code (e.g., COMC for corporate contribution, FIN5 for financial assistance, MINE/CNF for cross-border media and advertising services). The receiving bank will ask for the inward remittance advice and may require a sworn capital contribution declaration or legal opinion when the share subscription involves non-resident shareholders. All injections should be reconciled against corporate records, and inbound cross-border amounts above normal thresholds will trigger enhanced AML review; therefore the corporation should pre-advise its relationship manager and provide funding-source documentation before the wire.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: For media buy settlements and affiliate payouts, the primary clearing rails are: (i) domestic Canadian wire via the Large Value Transfer System (LVTS) for CAD-denominated payments; (ii) SWIFT MT103 international wire for cross-border USD, CAD, GBP, and EUR payments to ad networks, publisher partners, and media exchanges; (iii) Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS) via EFT/ACH for low-value recurring domestic payments; and (iv) commercial letters of credit for any supplier requiring payment security, though LCs are less common for performance media since the underlying service is intangible and not a documentary trade. The outbound treasury policy should bilaterally net confirmed media liabilities and maintain segregated disbursement accounts to reduce wire counts. For SWIFT MT103, use standard field 70 (Remittance Information) with invoice or contract reference, and field 50A/K for initiating account. Where possible, use SWIFT GPI to ensure same-day tracking. To minimize FX conversion leakage, hold USD receipts in a USD clearing account and disburse USD directly to U.S. ad networks rather than converting via CAD.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable spot CAD/USD contracts for immediate conversion settlement
Outright deliverable forward contracts (plain vanilla FX forwards up to 12 months) with a Schedule I Canadian bank or authorized derivatives dealer
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) executed offshore where CAD settlement is not feasible, subject to OSFI-compliant margin treatment and clear-board eligibility recommendations
Cross-currency swaps for medium-term matching of USD receivables and CAD operating expenses
FX options purchased (but not written) for downside cap on large media buy commitments
Embedded liquidity hedging through dual-currency multicurrency bank accounts permitting intraday natural netting and zero conversion windows

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due annually on the corporation's anniversary date, based on the incorporation or registration date.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: The prescribed filing fee is CAD 30, converted approximately to USD 22 at variable exchange rates. Failure to file may result in non-compliance notices and administrative dissolution or strike-off after two consecutive annual returns remain outstanding; restoration may require an application and additional fees.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal CBCA Annual Return, if the corporation is federally incorporated
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within 60 days after the corporation's anniversary date each year.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No government filing fee applies. Failure to file annual returns for two consecutive years may result in administrative dissolution; restoration requires compliance with outstanding filings and applicable restoration procedures.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: For a private Alberta corporation, there is generally no revenue, asset, or employee threshold that independently triggers a statutory audit. An auditor is generally required unless a valid shareholder exemption or waiver is available under the applicable corporate statute and shareholder resolution requirements. Publicly accountable corporations and entities subject to financing, securities, contractual, or regulatory requirements generally require an independent audit.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian GAAP applies. IFRS is mandatory for publicly accountable enterprises; eligible private corporations generally may use Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE), subject to applicable statutory, lender, investor, and contractual requirements.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: An Alberta corporation should maintain current internal records identifying individuals who directly or indirectly control the corporation and update ownership, control, and nominee information promptly after changes. Alberta generally has no separate annual public UBO confirmation filing. If federally incorporated under the CBCA, individuals-with-significant-control information must be maintained, reviewed annually, and reported through the federal annual return and on specified corporate changes.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control, where applicable
Minute Book containing shareholder and director resolutions and meeting minutes
Articles, bylaws, incorporation documents, amendments, and filed annual returns

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: Approximately USD 250-900 annually for registered office, records-office, and corporate service provider support; Alberta corporations generally do not require a separate statutory registered agent.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: Approximately USD 2,000-8,000 for a small private corporation, depending on transaction volume, revenue, consolidation, accounting records, and audit complexity.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined (15% federal general corporate rate + 8% Alberta general corporate rate); 11% combined (9% federal + 2% Alberta) on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income when the taxpayer qualifies as a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC).
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No statutory tax holiday applies to the digital advertising and media-buying sector. Available incentives include the federal Small Business Deduction (CCPC: 9% federal rate on up to CAD 500,000 of active business income), the Alberta Small Business Deduction (2% provincial rate on the same income), the 13% federal General Rate Reduction for non-CCPC taxable income, and refundable or non-refundable SR&ED investment tax credits (35% refundable for qualifying CCPCs; 15% non-refundable for large corporations). The former Alberta Digital Media Tax Credit is discontinued for new certifications; no sectoral exemption exists.
